title: The spider and the web; the hair on the body; the plants from the earth (1.1)
hook: how does one imperishable thing become a whole world? the Mundaka answers with three pictures from any backyard

segments.voice: Yesterday: the two knowledges, the lower that knows about, the higher that grasps the imperishable, akshara. Did you catch yourself knowing all about something you hadn't tasted? Day four hundred twelve.

Early morning, a garden. Between two branches there's a web that wasn't there last night, wet with dew, every thread catching light. And somewhere near the middle sits its maker, who brought no materials. No wood, no wire, no thread from a store. The whole thing came out of the spider's own body. Angiras has just told Shaunaka about the imperishable. The obvious next question is how one changeless thing could turn into everything we see. And instead of a theory, the Mundaka gives three pictures. The first is that spider.
screen: `A WEB THAT WASN'T THERE LAST NIGHT.` → `NO MATERIALS BROUGHT IN.` → `THREE PICTURES.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse. Yathorna-nabhih srijate grihnate cha. As a spider sends out its thread and draws it back in. As plants spring up from the earth. As hair grows on the head and body of a living person. So, from the imperishable, everything here comes into being. Three pictures, and each one teaches something different. The spider: the world doesn't come from some second stuff outside the source. The web is spun from the spider itself, and it can be drawn back in. The plants: the world rises naturally, the way green comes up after rain, without anybody pushing. And the hair: it grows from a living person without that person thinking about it at all. You don't decide to grow your eyebrows. So the source isn't straining. The world comes out of it the way hair comes out of you. Then the next verses add: through tapas, through that focused heat, Brahman swells, and from it comes food, from food breath, mind, truth, the worlds, and in action, the deathless. And the one who knows all, whose very tapas is made of knowledge, gives rise to name, form and food. Teachers read the spider differently. Advaita teachers say the web is an appearance, and the spider alone is ultimately real. Ramanuja's school reads the world as truly Brahman's own body, real and dependent. Madhva's school reads Brahman as the independent cause of a world that stays distinct from it. All three keep the spider. Even the Sanskrit word is a small picture: urnanabhi, spider, joins urna, thread or wool, and nabhi, navel.
screen: `AS A SPIDER SPINS AND DRAWS BACK.` · `AS PLANTS RISE FROM THE EARTH.` · `AS HAIR GROWS WITHOUT TRYING.` · `SO, FROM THE IMPERISHABLE, ALL THIS.` · then, large: `URNANABHI.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the three pictures. Sit, and feel your breath go out like a thread, and come back in. Out, and drawn back. That's the spider. Then notice something growing in you without your effort: your hair, your nails, the steady beat of the heart. That's the hair. Then let thoughts rise and fall on their own, the way plants come up from the ground, without pushing them. Rest at the center, where the thread comes from. The bell holds the time.
Urnanabhi, the spider. The Mundaka's picture of a world spun from its own source, as naturally as plants from the earth and hair from a living body.
Your line: as the spider. Today, when you see a web, or a plant pushing through a crack, let it remind you of the Mundaka's three pictures. Day four hundred twelve.

howItsDone: The spider verse of Mundaka 1.1.7 is a standard teaching text in Vedanta, and teachers of different schools explain it in class to show how they understand the relation between Brahman and the world.

fork.setup: you need to explain how one changeless source becomes a whole world, to a student, in one verse. what do you use?
options: a potter shaping clay he bought.
a spider, plants from the earth, and hair on a body.
a battle between gods and demons.
fork.reveal: the Mundaka uses three pictures: a spider spinning from itself, plants rising, hair growing, and says so from the imperishable comes all this.

original.note: Sanskrit ūrṇanābhi, spider: ūrṇā, wool or thread, + nābhi, navel. Mundaka 1.1.7.

trapdoor: what you thought: creation means someone building with materials.
what it means: in the Mundaka, the world comes from the imperishable the way a web comes from a spider, plants from earth, hair from a body.
what a scholar hears: yathorṇanābhiḥ sṛjate gṛhṇate ca (1.1.7); the spider image also appears in the Brihadaranyaka (2.1.20) and Shvetashvatara (6.10).

sources.ref: Mundaka Upanishad 1.1.8–1.1.9 (Brahman swells by tapas; name, form and food)
